utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day to all. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On behalf of the Judges, I would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom. And I would like to ask Mr. Scott to introduce his assistant who is sitting to his left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Joining me in the courtroom today is Tonia Gillett, an attorney also with the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. I won't ask for the appearances for the Defence counsel as nothing has changed. Today on the 29th of May, 2006, we will be calling in a witness. I'll now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what is being said. If so, please say that you can understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milivoj Gagro. I was born on the 2nd of June, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1992, 1993, and 1994, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I appear before the international court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And have you already testified before a national court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will show you the slip of paper now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information. As you are aware, you have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You will be testifying in the Prlic et al. case, as you're well aware. First you'll have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution, whom you have met when being proofed for this hearing, and once the examination-in-chief has been concluded, the Defence teams for the accused, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. If the need arises and if the accused believe it is in the interest of their defence, the accused may also put questions to you. The four Judges sitting before you may also at any point in time put questions to you. This is provided for in the Rules. For example, in the Nuremberg trials, it was possible for the Judges to put questions to the witness. Other international tribunals have proceeded in this manner. You will notice that the questions put to you can vary, depending on the party putting the question to you. The Prosecution will put questions that will be phrased in neutral terms. However, Defence counsel can put leading questions to you as a result of which you can answer by saying either yes or no. As far as the Judges are concerned, the nature of their questions is somewhat different. We are trying to establish what the truth is, or we're trying to obtain certain clarifications with regard to witness's testimony in the course of the examination-in-chief or in the course of the cross-examination. If you encounter any difficulties of any kind, please inform us of the fact. You have taken the solemn declaration. You have sworn to speak the truth, which means that you should not give false testimony, but you are well aware of the fact. In addition, every one and a half hours we will have a 20-minute break. At about 1530 we will have a 20-minute break, and today it is necessary to conclude by 7.00 p.m. Without wasting any more time, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution who will commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: 2nd of June, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I thought perhaps it was in the record, but in case it was not, would you again state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: My name is Milivoj Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I was born in Hodbine, which is near Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, do you identify yourself as a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to briefly take you through some of your personal background, both educational and professional background. If I understand correctly, sir, you received a degree in civil engineering from the University of Zagreb in 1969. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you served a period of military service with the JNA during the approximate time 1967 to 1968; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And upon receiving your -- upon being discharged from the JNA and receiving your degree, you went to Mostar in approximately 1969, or returned to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from approximately 1969 to 1990, you were employed at the Institute of Urban Planning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That brings us up, then, to 1990. Around that time, sir, did you become involved in political matters in the Mostar area, 1989, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to specify what sort of political matters I was involved in. Perhaps you could clarify your question and be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you become involved in a political party known as the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that capacity or as part of that -- as part of your involvement in that party, did you run for the Mostar municipal -- for a position or a seat in the Mostar Municipal Assembly in the multi-party elections in December, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you successful in being elected to the Mostar Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the HDZ list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, do you recall approximately how many seats comprise the Mostar Municipal Assembly as of that time, December, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The Assembly was supposed to elect 100 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell the Judges, of those 100 seats, approximately how many seats did the HDZ party win as a result of those elections?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: At those first multi-party elections, the HDZ obtained 30 seats in the Mostar Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you obtained one of those seats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: One of those seats was mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the transcript on line 5 the answer is given as, "The Assembly was supposed to elect 100 members." Is that correct or is it to have 100 members?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, did you hear the Judge's question, and could you possibly clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: According to the electoral programme, a hundred members of the Assembly were supposed to be elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can come at it this way, sir: Was the Municipal Assembly at that time composed of approximately 100 seats or positions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: One hundred seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, in addition to being elected as a member of the Assembly at this time, did you then subsequently become, or as part of this process become selected as the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. It was organised in a somewhat different manner at the time. A president of the Assembly would be elected, president of the Municipal Assembly, and in that capacity he had the competence of a mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, please explain to the Judges in your own words the process by which you became the mayor of Mostar in approximately 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: After the Assembly had been constituted, after the mandates had been confirmed for the Mostar Municipal Assembly, at the first constituent session the most senior member of the Assembly presided over the debates, and there was an inter-party agreement, and the most senior member would determine all the functions of importance for that Assembly. So at that session of the Assembly, an HDZ member was proposed as the Assembly president, and that was myself. There was a different representative proposed for the SDS and for the SDA. They had the president of the Executive Board elected. Those three positions were voted on, and all three candidates were elected to those positions at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as part of this election, who was allowed, then, to cast votes for these three positions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: All 100 Assembly members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So all the -- all the members of the Assembly, whether they be from the SDA, from the HDZ, from the SDS, or any other party, were allowed to participate in this election; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. They all had the right to one vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell the Judges, then, how long did you remain in the position of mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I was appointed at that first session held towards the end of 1990, and I held that office until around the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us that you were a member of the HDZ party at the time you were elected. Who was the president of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time of your election?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Kljujic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the time of your election Mr. Perinovic had been replaced by Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljujic is someone I had never met before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Perinovic had been the first president of the party, of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why had he been removed from that position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, those who had a lot of influence in HDZ were informed that this person wasn't a full Croat, and as a result he could not adequately represent the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges if he was not "full Croat," what else was he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: He was a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what other ethnic group in Bosnia and Herzegovina had Mr. Perinovic been identified with, which apparently caused him to lose his position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how -- what process was followed in naming Stjepan Kljujic as party president to replace Mr. Perinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how long Mr. Kljujic remained as president of the HDZ, or do you recall -- let me ask it this way, if it assists you: Do you recall when approximately Mr. Kljujic ceased being president of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, that was towards the end of 1991, at a party meeting held in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, there was a party of a similar name, the Croatian Democratic Union in the Republic of Croatia -- excuse me, Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. We called it the Sestrina Party; the Sister Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what relationship, if any, existed between the HDZ party in Croatia and the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, there was a relationship. There's no doubt about that. Without their assistance, it would have been very difficult for the HDZ to organise itself in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who in the Croatian party, the HDZ, did -- did it appear to you was most involved in dealings with the party in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Susak was most involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Susak was the minister of defence of Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any dealings or meetings with Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you know of the nature of the dealings or meetings, communications between the party in Zagreb, that is the HDZ party in Zagreb, and the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: There were consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, after you were elected as mayor of Mostar and through your in the HDZ party, did you become aware of a difference in views between a part of the party which may have been represented by Mr. Kljujic and another part of the party represented perhaps by Mr. Boban, Mr. Kordic, and people in that group?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. This became obvious during a period of time that preceded the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Judges the basic differences of positions or views between Mr. Kljujic on the one hand and Mr. Boban and others on the other?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, the main difference was that those who lived in multi-ethnic areas believed that it was necessary to support the idea of co-existence, to nurture this idea, whereas in areas where only one ethnic group lived, well, they thought that this was a secondary matter and they thought that their objectives could be pursued without trying to reach agreements with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You've identified two points of view. Can you tell us which of those two points of view was held by Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. He was in favour for a single and indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what view do you associate Mr. Boban with of the two views that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, he believed that many things or many ideas developed in Sarajevo were not suitable to the area in which he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what did -- what did Mr. Boban want to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, some form of autonomy for the area in which the Croatian population was in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during this time that you were a member of the HDZ and the mayor of Mostar, did you observe that Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Boban came into increasing conflict because of these different views?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They would very rarely meet towards the end, and when they tried to find a common language, it was very difficult. One would try to find some other body that would be capable of reconciling the varying positions that were irreconcilable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Given the division in the party, sir, can you tell the Judges, for example, how would it be that if Mr. Boban hoped to accomplish a particular objective or reach a particular decision, given the split in the party, what sort of activities he would engage in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Whoever was not ready to cooperate with him, well, such a person would be eliminated or, rather, he would try to remove such a person from the position that he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I ask you, sir, in terms of these positions that we've been talking about for the last few minutes, where did you put yourself in the time period 1990, 1991, 1992? What position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm from Mostar, from a multi-ethnic area, and co-existence was something that was valued. This has been the case throughout history, and we could not support an idea according to which it was necessary to establish divisions. At the time, those were my beliefs, and I stand by those beliefs to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct your attention forward to a time in 1991. Did you attend a meeting in Zagreb involving perhaps Mr. Tudjman and others to discuss various policies and matters related to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I only attended one meeting which was organised with the Bosnian Croats, and I attended that meeting. That meeting was chaired by Mr. Susak. Mr. Tudjman came at the end, just to say hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall the approximate date of this meeting in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember the exact date now, but the meeting might have been sometime in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what was discussed at this meeting? Well, first of all, can you tell us a bit more about how you came to be actually invited to this meeting? What series of events led up to you being invited to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago we were saying that our options were different and that we had different views as to how the Croatian question in Bosnia-Herzegovina ought to be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me more about how you actually came to be invited to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I was left out of an invitation to a meeting of a group of Croatian leaders which was in Herzegovina, and then subsequently they sent out an invitation and asked me to attend the Bosnian group which had rallied in Zagreb one week later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Kljujic about these events and the scheduling of the two meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because Mr. Kljujic attended that first meeting, and he was surprised not to see me there, the meeting of the Herzegovina Croats. And he objected and asked why I hadn't been invited, so they invited me subsequently with the Bosnian group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this conversation with Mr. Kljujic, did Mr. Kljujic tell you about -- anything about another -- a second meeting that he had been involved in after meeting with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you in fact then go to this second meeting, or the meeting that you were invited to? Before that - sorry - were you given any explanation to as to why -- did you ever ask him -- were you given any explanation as to why you hadn't been invited to the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, to Mr. Kljujic's reaction, the answer they gave him was that they weren't able to find him -- find me. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say Mr. Kljujic's reaction, they gave him -- "the answer they gave him," who gave him that answer? Who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The representatives of the Herzegovacka group [phoen] who organised the meeting in Zagreb. I think it was Mr. Maric who took it upon himself to organise the meeting and to go to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall or had you done anything during that time to make yourself unavailable at this earlier time, during the first meeting that you were not included in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, not that I was unavailable. I assume - I can't be sure - that they wanted to avoid me coming to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why would they want to avoid you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, we were talking about a moment ago and saying that in fact my position and my attitude that Mostar must remain a multi-ethnic town, that we should build it up that way, did not suit people who didn't think like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you did go to the second meeting, the one apparently you said chaired by Mr. Susak, with President Tudjman coming in toward the end, what was the nature or the topic of discussions -- excuse me, the topics of discussion at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Very serious topics, because it was already a period when a bloody war was raging in Croatia, and we were almost certain that the same thing awaited the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was under those circumstances that we expected something to happen or, rather, that was already going on in Croatia, because we understood the very grave situation we were faced with, and an answer was being sought to the question of how to protect Croatian citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you make any proposal at that meeting about the creation of something called a Community of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, in my statement which was presented here, it says that I said that I proposed that, but in fact what I said is this: I said I supported it. I supported the idea of creating a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I think that was a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your idea of this community that you supported at that time? Would it be a -- would it have a government, or what was the nature of this community association that you gave your support to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, not a government or any separate organisation. Quite simply, the Croats lived and still live today, unfortunately, dispersed all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this great dispersion of the population broke up a necessary continuity and communication among the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why we sought a solution. We looked into the ways and means of solving certain vital issues for survival of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I thought that that would be the best solution, given the situation that we were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were any concrete resolutions reached at this meeting in terms of what would actually be done, what steps would be taken to accomplish this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. As I have already repeated here and in my statement, too, they were consultations that were held, and altogether we sought the best solutions. And after the meeting, we were given the assignment of going to implement the conclusions, and it was the duty and obligation of all people that attended the meeting and anybody else who could help them in implementing the decisions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, sir, subsequently to this time attend a meeting in Grude on about the 12th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that was a meeting held to see how to give shape to the solutions that we had agreed upon in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00071.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that document is, and does this relate to the meeting that you just mentioned a moment ago on the 12th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it does relate to that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask -- direct your attention to the last page of that document, which is a list of -- a page of signatures. And if you have that, sir, if you can look at number 22. Is that your name and your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name and my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at that document, sir, if you look at the number -- signature number 1 or name number 1, can you tell us whose name that appears to be? I direct your attention in particular out to the far right end of that line.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a couple of others by example. Number 14 is Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you assist us, please, with who signed at number 18?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you look -- keeping that page in mind, sir, when you signed that as number 22, when you signed that document, did you understand that you were signing a document in the sense of giving your endorsement or approval to something that had been said before this, or what was your understanding of the document, of the page of which you put your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. I think the matter is quite clear. At our meeting, which was held quite late, the first thing we did was to write down the names of all those present and sign that, give our signatures. Now, when discussing how to define the conclusions that we had been preparing, well, there was a long discussion about that, and it was said that we would give our conclusions subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did you first learn that something called "Conclusions" had been apparently typed up and circulated or publicised?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Kljujic called me up the next day and asked me how I had agreed to that kind of statement and to putting my signature to that kind of thing. I was surprised and denied that my signature was placed after a statement that had been read out which was attached to our signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that in mind, if I can direct your attention, with the registry's assistance, back to the first page of the document and the section that's numbered paragraph number 1. First of all, sir, when you look at that, you see there are references to two meetings in Zagreb, one on the 13th and one on the 20th of June, 1991. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does that assist you in putting a date on the meeting that you told us about a few moments ago when you attended the meeting chaired by Mr. Susak in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It says the 20th of June -- of -- yes, June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not asking what it says so much, sir, but I'm saying does that assist you in putting the date on the meeting that you attended in Zagreb that you told us about a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I think that's the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to the end of that paragraph, that same paragraph in which the dates are mentioned, and it contains this language: "These two regional communities have jointly and unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally carry out a decisive and active policy which should lead to the realisation of our centuries old dream, a joint Croatian state." Now, sir, going back to what you were saying a few moments ago, did you -- had you endorsed and did you agree with that statement? Was that your position, your personal position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to paragraph numbered 2. Do you also recall whether or not in this meeting there was discussion -- parts of the leadership of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina which held a different view, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was quite obvious. A different approach to many who had taken part in the creation of decisions that were to govern the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning the persons being referenced in paragraph number 2, did that include Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kljujic, and, I'll tell you, me too; yours truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it was -- I think the evidence will show and there will probably not be any dispute that about six days later, on the 18th of November, 1991, the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was declared. And did you attend the meeting at which that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge did Mr. Kljujic attend the meeting where the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was declared?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how it was that the -- how the particular individuals that came to that meeting -- that did attend that meeting, how they came to be invited or included whereas others were not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. Simply because someone didn't attend does not mean that he wasn't invited, and I think the question assumes a fact not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, would you restate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'll ask you only if you have some information that can assist us. Did you -- did you learn at the time or did you have any understanding as to how it was that some people attended the meeting -- this particular meeting on the 18th of November, and those like Mr. Kljujic and yourself who did not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I don't think they invited me, because I said quite clearly that I didn't agree with that kind of conclusion and those decisions and that Mr. Kljujic said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the -- you mentioned this earlier, but can you tell the Judges any more now about whether Mr. Kljujic was removed or withdrew from the party Presidency around this time or following the declaration of the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I think that would be right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know from conversations or from your relationship with Mr. Kljujic why he either was removed or took himself out of that position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm going to object. First we need a clarification. Was he -- did he withdraw or was he removed? There are two different concepts there. Then he can answer the following question. But I think it's -- I don't want to say misleading, but it's confusing later on when we try to figure out what exactly happened to Mr. Kljujic based on this gentleman's understanding and memory, and of course his prior statement that we all know what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy, Your Honour, to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, can you tell us your understanding of when Mr. Kljujic ceased being actively -- at least actively the president of the HDZ party in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know how that came about in general terms? That is, was he fired by someone? Was he discharged? Did he essentially withdraw himself from the position, or can you assist the Judges in how that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, everything culminated, the disagreements between Grude and Sarajevo, and this was resolved by calling an expanded session of the board of the Croatian Democratic Union, and that meeting, according to Kljujic's interpretation, he said he didn't convene that. As party president, he was the only one in the proper place to do so. But anyway, he did go to the meeting, but although he was there physically, he didn't want to chair the meeting or make the opening address, and that's when they ran up against a serious problem of finding who was best placed to declare the meeting open and present the agenda. A solution was found, and the host, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Siroki Brijeg, went up to the rostrum and invited Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Boban to take their seats as the president and vice-president of the party. Both men agreed, and they sat down to the table and the discussion began. After that, Mr. Maric, from Grude, asked to take the floor, and in his presentation he hurled a number of accusations and made a number insinuations against Mr. Kljujic, who couldn't stand hearing this and listening to it, and demonstrably got up and said, "No. I am going to resign," and he left the meeting. So that is how Mr. Kljujic, declaring his own will and in an angry tone to demonstrate his dissatisfaction, left the meeting, which in my view, was the aim of the gentleman from Grude. They wanted to provoke him so that he took precisely that step.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, just before we get too much further along, just so the record is clear, a moment ago you said, looking back at page 21, around line 11, "... invited Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Boban to take their seats as the president and vice-president..." Is it correct, sir, that at this time Mr. Kljujic, as you've already indicated, was the party president and Mr. Boban was the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, I failed to ask you a moment ago when I asked you who attended the meeting on the 18th of November, 1991, where the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was declared, I asked you if Mr. Kljujic attended that meeting. You said no. I didn't -- I failed to ask you, do you know whether Mr. Kljujic supported the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as declared on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. I can't give you a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, once Mr. Kljujic had taken this step of indicating that he was willing to resign, was anyone named at that time to replace Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when someone named Milenko Brkic was named or put in the position, at least, as acting president of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. In fact, he did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, not president -- perhaps I misspoke. Not president of the meeting, not presiding officer at the meeting, but in terms of the political party of HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was Mr. Brkic subsequently selected in some fashion to be acting president in place of Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. He was never even considered for the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who took the position after Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. For a long time there was a vacuum in this process, and eventually Professor Milenko Brkic was nominated, and he accepted to be nominated. I believe that this was about a month or two after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know how long Mr. Brkic remained in that position, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Three to four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know who followed Mr. Brkic as party president of the HDZ-BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Kordic assumed that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is a little break, it seems. There is one point that I don't know whether I misunderstood or missed something. Did you, Mr. Gagro, attend that meeting which Kljujic left? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did attend it. I was there. Actually, I was his host. He first came to Mostar to complain to me, then I escorted him to that meeting, but he didn't say good-bye to me when he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to a different topic, sir. The city of Mostar, in your -- in these various meetings and your involvement with the HDZ, do you know that when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was declared Mostar was declared as the capital of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall any meetings with any other political officials and anyone from the Serb side, if you will, the Serb ethnic group, who ever expressed a view to you about Mostar being the Croatian capital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, yes. This was already a stage when roadblocks were being erected. Everyone was showing their force and demonstrating their dissatisfaction, and whenever people wished to sever communications, I wrote, they did so very easily according to the fashion of the so-called log revolution. So such an untenable state with such roadblocks featuring required a solution. Mr. Koljevic came to visit us in Mostar, Mr. Koljevic, a representative of the Serbs on behalf of Mr. Karadzic, and so we tried to find a way out of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I just ask if you know what Mr. Koljevic's position -- you said he represented Mr. Karadzic. Do you know what Mr. Koljevic's position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That is a difficult question. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, though, with your answer. I apologise for interrupting you. What did Mr. Koljevic say about this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the situation generally required us to find a final solution to put an end to the agony which had befallen Bosnia-Herzegovina. We sought to find such solutions as would be satisfactory for all the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina without a conflict erupting, and at a certain point he said, "Well, here, look here, we Serbs are really for Mostar to be in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when this meeting occurred or this conversation occurred with Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, it might have taken place in November or December. We were deep into autumn, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And which year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It was 1991. It was 1991. The Titograd Uzice Corps had already been -- was already present in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting you, but there is an error in the transcript, so can we please clarify this. It's line 24 -- page 24, line 19. The witness said that Koljevic told him that the Serbs agreed for Mostar to be a Croatian town, whereas the transcript says that they agreed -- that the Serbs agreed that Mostar should be in Croatia, in the State of Croatia instead of saying that it be Croatian. There's a significance difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you perhaps clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me? What he said was that the Serbs didn't have anything against Mostar being Croatian. And let me add to that the Croats -- the Croatian centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, by the time we get to this point, you've just said this was approximately in November, December, 1991, had JNA and the Serb forces come into the Mostar area in a substantial way in approximately September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. They came on the 19th of September in 1991, under the designation the Titograd Uzice Corps. Replying to our question why they were there, they said they were there to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by the time we get into approximately March of 1992, what positions did the Serbs hold or the JNA hold in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: 1993, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the spring or late winter, spring of 1992; March, April of 1992, what positions or line did they hold in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: If you let me explain the real reason for the arrival of this corps, then I'd have to say this: Slovenia had already gone through the conflicts in Slovenia, whereas a bloody war was raging in Croatia. All the forces of the JNA could pull out from Slovenia and partly from Croatia. It did not withdraw to Serbia and Montenegro but actually deployed them in their locations around Mostar. They had elaborated a definite tactic as to how to secure their positions, and most tragically, from those positions they heavily shelled Croatia as well. So that the reaction of the local populace was to actually consider them an occupying force and an enemy that was actually tearing -- razing to the ground Croatian soil. And that is the source of this conflict which later then escalated into this horrendous tragedy that we had to go through. First, initially they sought to defend their airports and their barracks on a wide front, but as matters developed or, rather, escalated in the negative direction, they kept spreading so that they actually oversaw the positions towards Citluk, towards Siroki Brijeg, towards Zitomislici, and other parts around Mostar, so they had control of that area. We were already then under a complete blockade and the only road allowing for an exit from the city was in the direction of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the toponym.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This actually sowed an enormous degree of discord amongst the ethnic communities in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I note the interpreter is having some difficulty, and one of Mr. Gagro's microphones is not on, it appears. Maybe if someone could assist him. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, during this time, sir, the Serbs, the JNA forces being in Herzegovina, sometime during that period was something called the Mostar Crisis Staff created?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it was. According to the statute of the Municipal Assembly of Mostar, in the event of the imminent threat of war and when legal authorities are unable to properly function, all the powers of the legal authorities are then vested into a single organisation, a single house, as it were, which is to say they are rallied within a Crisis Staff which then decides on all spheres of life and activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges approximately, sir, when the Crisis Staff was established in Mostar of which you were a part?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I believe that it was already sometime mid-March that we had to relocate ourselves, to withdraw from our civilian work posts into an atomic shelter which ensured the security of the operation of our Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you mark that time as the time when the Crisis Staff had been established, or referring you to again, you said on the 19th of September, I believe, is when the JNA -- 1991, is when the JNA came into the Mostar region. Let me ask you again: Do you recall approximately when the Crisis Staff was first established?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I believe that I recall the time more or less exactly. It might have been a month before that or a month later. Perhaps it was in February, but at any rate, it was after -- in late 1991 and early 1992 that matters culminated to such an extent that it was impossible to normally live and work in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was the Crisis Staff, the Mostar Crisis Staff comprised? Who made up this Crisis Staff? Not necessarily particular individuals, although you're free to give names if you like, but how was it established and what people, what positions were created?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had a number of staff. I don't know how -- on what basis that was defined, but according to the positions as deputies, the Croats got four places on the Crisis Staff, the Muslims three, and the Serbs two places, and these vacancies were filled with such a number. They were filled up on the principle of the participation, the share of the individual respective parties in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your position on the Crisis Staff? Were you the head of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. I remained at the helm of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, a little bit more about what the function of the Crisis Staff was. What sort of activities or efforts did the Crisis Staff engage in during this time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: In that chaotic situation, basically, and as far as realistically possible, we strove to make the situation as painless for the people as possible. As we saw that there were -- the destruction of the city lay in store, the first task that we wanted to address was to get the sufficient number of bags and to organise shelters in the housing units where the people were living. The second task that we carried out was to ensure regular supplies of basic necessities for the populace. And thirdly, also to ensure a semblance of peace, because under such abnormal circumstances, of course, lawlessness was rife, and people pursued their own selfish interests in such a context. So we tried to carry out these duties through our individual activities, and it functioned for a period of time. We were satisfied during that period to have been able to actually properly deal with the major problems that we were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the same time, did the Mostar Municipal Assembly, the body that you had first been elected to in 1990, did the Municipal Assembly continue to meet and function during this time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. I only know that there have been a plan to hold one meeting of that Municipal Assembly, to convene it for a meeting, but since the conditions did not permit, no such meeting was convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the registry to please display to the witness and in the courtroom Exhibit P 00135. We can stop now, Your Honour, or whichever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll stop now and we'll resume at five to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, right before the break I was about to ask the registry to please display to you Exhibit P 00135. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes. Yes. I see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is this a document dated the 12th of March, 1992, by which you called a meeting of the Mostar Municipal Assembly, calling a meeting for the 16th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but obviously it lacks my signature. In fact, this meeting was not held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The seal that is on the document, on the Croatian language original, is that the -- that is the seal of your office, as far as you can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the agenda item number 2, the first item, you talk about resigning of members of the Mostar municipality Executive Board. Is there anything that you can remember and tell the Judges about what that was about? What members were resigning and, if you recall, why?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Under the circumstances I described before: The SDS, the Serbs' party, decided to recall its members from the Executive Board, so there remained vacancies which they had occupied before, and we wanted to fill those vacancies with other people, and that was to be discussed at the Municipal Assembly session and a decision adopted on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me ask you a similar question about the second item under agenda item 2, resigning of chiefs of security service centres. What was happening in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Also to fill the posts made vacant by people who had withdrawn. But in fact, in this case their leadership asked them to withdraw from the organs of authority of the city of Mostar, from the government of the city of Mostar. If you allow me, perhaps I could relate a detail that is of some interest. Savo Zimonjic was my vice-president on behalf of the SDS. Once he told me that he had been invited to their staff, and they asked him, "Savo, will you opt for them or for us?" Unfortunately, that was the policy the SDS pursued in Mostar, and that was the manner in which these people were recalled from the government organs in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to the Crisis Staff, as opposed to the Municipal Assembly which is reflected on this particular document, going back to the points of view that we were discussing earlier this afternoon and the difference between Mr. Kljujic on the one hand and Mr. Boban on the other, can you tell the Judges whether the views of the Mostar Crisis Staff at this time, that is in March, April, 1992, did they coincide more with your views and Mr. Kljujic's views, or did they coincide with Mr. Boban's views?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: They didn't coincide with Boban's views or with Kljujic's views. We defined matters on the basis of our own ideas, on the basis of the ideas we had with regard to how the town and our local commune should function.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, around this time in April of 1992, was the Croatian Defence Council, or HVO, established?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Could you specify the time you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall, sir, approximately, just in general, how did you become aware of the establishment of the HVO? How did its existence first come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: We were in contact with people who were responsible for the defence of the town. After some time had passed -- or, rather, first we called our own defence forces the defence forces for the town of Mostar. And then after some time had passed, after a short period of time, those forces were renamed the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn at some time that some structure had been established that was similar to the Crisis Staff other than the military forces as you just described them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to please be shown Exhibit P 00157.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This previous document ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have that document, if I could direct your attention to the -- I believe it would be the sixth paragraph of that document starting with the words -- starting with the word "Reminding ..." If you could please find that. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That paragraph states: "Reminding that at the time the term used for such organisations was Crisis Staffs, Boban said that, 'Actually, nothing new has been created. It is just the renaming of the former Crisis Staffs, giving them a new adequate Croatian designation.'" Were you informed any time around that time - that is the first half of April 1992 - that the Mostar Crisis Staff, of which you were the head, had been renamed the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention next to Exhibit P 00180. If you have that, sir, can you tell the Judges what that is as you understand it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Given the undefined situation that Mostar was in, given the ambiguous situation it was in, it was necessary to determine who the aggressor was and who represented the defence, and this is a way in which we wanted to determine the roles all the parties were playing. We wanted to determine who the aggressor was if the defence was represented by the defence forces of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a document -- or a decision dated the 29th of April, 1992. And if you will look at the version that you have in front of you, does it bear your name and signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you signed this document about the 29th of April, 1992, what did you understand the thrust of this document to be? What did it -- what did it -- what powers or direction did it give to the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I think that the document is quite clear about the purpose of this decision. We had been attacked, and we were looking for a way to defend ourselves. All the forces that were available were forces that we tried to avail ourselves of. We tried to organise them to defend Mostar, which was in a very difficult position. In item I, we said that the Yugoslav People's Army and other paramilitary formations acting together with it were declared as enemy forces and an occupying formation in the territory of the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say in section -- Article number II, "The Croat Defence Council municipal headquarters Mostar," who did you understand to be or how was that body comprised as of the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, the only forces that we had for the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you understand about the continued role of the Mostar Crisis Staff and the Mostar Municipal Assembly under this agreement or decision?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The role was clearly defined. It was to defend the town and to liberate the town from those who were attacking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me restate my question, and listen, please. I'm not asking now about the role of the HVO specifically. What was the role, the role envisaged of the Mostar Crisis Staff and the Mostar Municipal Assembly under this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat this: They have two tasks; to prevent the aggressor from taking control of Mostar and, if possible, to expel these forces from Mostar, to liberate the town. So the aggressor was to be driven out of Mostar, and this was the exclusive military task of the military formation that we had in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did this decision remove the Mostar Municipal Assembly and remove the Mostar Crisis Staff from the civilian or executive administrative authority in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Do you mean did we quite simply extinguish ourselves? No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me give you a specific example. If I can direct your attention to -- excuse me -- Article number VII. If you'll find that, please. And in the first sentence of Article VII, it says that: "The HVO shall coordinate with the municipal Crisis Staff." How were you going -- how was the municipal Crisis Staff, the Mostar Crisis Staff, going to coordinate with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, we had to approve their activities. They couldn't act without being subject to the control of the civilian authorities. They had to be subordinated to the civilian authorities, whatever form these authorities took. At the time, it was the Crisis Staff of the Mostar Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at the second sentence of Article VII: "The questions of common interest shall be resolved at joint sessions of the Crisis headquarters of the Assembly and the Croat Defence Council." Do you recall any time in April or May, 1992, sir, when there was any joint session of the Mostar Crisis Staff or Municipal Assembly and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On Article VIII, if I can direct your attention to Article VIII, please. It indicates that: "The Crisis headquarters -- or Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar shall establish as soon as possible the temporary Executive Council, which will ensure the functioning of the government bodies." Did the -- either the Municipal Assembly or the Mostar Crisis Staff ever have an opportunity to establish these executive government bodies following this decision on the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That was what we ardently desired. We wanted to return to some kind of a normal life, but everything escalated and we were unable to establish some sort of departments that would function as -- or, rather, represent the civilian local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us a few minutes ago that the Serb members of these bodies had been resigning or withdrawing from these bodies as of the end of April, early part of May, 1992. Were the Muslim members, the Muslim representatives on these bodies still participating in these bodies at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. There's just -- I think there's a need to put a more precise question to the witness when he talks about "bodies." "Bodies" has a wide meaning. Is he referring to departments, or is he referring to an Assembly? Because we have a Crisis Staff of the Assembly, of the Municipal Assembly, not to be confused with Crisis Staff and Municipal Assembly and now we're talking about "bodies." So perhaps we could have a more precise question so the witness can precisely give us his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott, please put precise questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, at the time of this decision, which is dated and signed by you about the 29th of April, 1992, were there still active members of the Mostar Municipal Assembly who were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Crisis Staff? Could you please clarify this for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was the Mostar Municipal Assembly. If it will assist you, perhaps you can direct your attention back to -- if I can have the usher's assistance to direct the witness to Exhibit P 00135. Do you have that document, sir? You have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, when you called this meeting -- when you sent this invitation for a meeting on the 12th of March, 1992, did some of the people that you invited include Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I think one has to say that the meeting wasn't held. We invited all those from the valid list of Assembly members. I don't know who was present, who could have responded to the invitation, et cetera, because this session was simply not held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question was not whether the session was held. You sent an invitation. You sent a call to a meeting. Did your call to the meeting including the Muslim members of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It was -- they were -- invitations were sent out to all the members. No one was forgotten. No Serbs, no Muslims, no Croats were forgotten, nor was anyone else who participated in the town Assembly. So a hundred invitations were sent out to the addresses of the members of the Assembly, the addresses that had been registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go -- direct your attention now specifically to the Mostar Crisis Staff. As of late April, 1992, and May, 1992, did the Mostar Crisis Staff at that time still include among its membership persons who were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. They remained in the Crisis Staff until the end and they took part in the Crisis Staff's activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, please, to Exhibit P 00190. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn around this time, the 7th of May, 1992, that the HVO had formed something called the Special Purpose Council of the Mostar Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I can see that it says "Confidential" here, but I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand that some other body had been set up to take the place of the Mostar Crisis Staff as of early May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No one informed us of the existence of such a new body that would take over the role of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you can assist us with this, sir: If this body was going to be involved in governing or administering Mostar, how could it be that its composition would remain confidential?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I really don't know. Perhaps there was a communications problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the witness has said he's never seen this document before, and I therefore think that there is no purpose if one tries to discuss the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, the witness can't recognise this document. He's told us that this is the first time he's seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question wasn't about the document any longer. What the witness said was he was never informed of there being some other body set up to essentially fulfil the role of the Crisis Staff, and my question is simply: How could such a governing body function if it remained confidential? It's nothing to do with whether he's seen this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question. I didn't object earlier but, again, there is some sort of a suggestion, it assumes a fact not in evidence that this body actually supplanted the Crisis Staff. And I guess if we would just go back to a traditional way of doing direct examination: Who, what, where, why, how, and explain, we won't run into those problems. But I think that the question, the way it's phrased, it assumes a fact not in evidence that somehow this document demonstrates that a body was set up to supplant the Crisis Staff. I don't see that from the document, but I think the gentleman should be asked questions if in fact something happened to the Crisis Staff, and he can tell us, he can give a narrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put the question to the witness myself. Sir, the Prosecution has shown you document P 190, according to which the HVO established a different body. Initially you said that you were completely ignorant of the establishment of such a body, or completely unaware of such a body. With regard to the Defence's objection, how could you explain the fact that a different structure, a different body was created behind your back without your being aware of it? If you have just found out about this today, what could you tell us about the matter to provide us with an explanation? How would you have experienced such a thing at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, reading through some of the tasks that have been listed here, I could say that these tasks could have been of assistance to the town's Crisis Staff. These tasks would have been welcomed. And it's not something I would perceive as being something done behind my back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was to assist you, why weren't you informed of the fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a problem I can't solve. I can't answer that question. Why was it confidential? Why wasn't the Crisis Staff informed of this fact? Why didn't the Crisis Staff verify this decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't see how one could explain the fact that this body was not one that you were informed of, and the members of the Crisis Staff were simply not informed of the existence of this body, although you said that it was for a good cause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness to be shown next Exhibit P 00199.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is this a document dated the 10th of May, 1992, by Mate Boban and Janko Bobetko, appointing various people to the Mostar Crisis -- excuse me, Mostar Municipal Staff, I believe it's described here.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, obviously I never received this document either. And so that is something that bypassed our control, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were still the democratically elected mayor of Mostar. You were still, as Mr. President has just indicated, you were still the head of the Mostar Crisis Staff. How could it be if this body was set up without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I really can't say. I have no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the second -- well, maybe on the first page of your document, but looking at the names at the bottom of the document, did you know that Janko Bobetko was a general or head of the Croatian army, the Republic of Croatia army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. We never accepted that nor approved it, and as far as I'm concerned, this is very disconcerting. I have no comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, why would a general in the Croatian army be signing a document appointing members of the Mostar Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Before we go on to look at the next exhibit, sir, let's imagine that the 10th of May, 1992, was the date when you learnt - you in your capacity of president of the Crisis Staff - that a Croatian general was signing a document putting into place a structure in the municipality of Mostar. What would you have done if you had learnt about this on the 10th of May, 1992? What would have been your reaction, and what would you have done, faced with that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing that I could have done was this: To ask for an explanation why and in what way this came about, why this document was passed and why it was signed by the people who signed it, who are the signatories at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you could direct the witness's -- to the attention that this is in regard to the Croatian Defence Council of Mostar, not anything to do with the Crisis Staff. And I think that's an important distinction that needs to be brought out during this discussion, that that's what we're talking about, the Croatian Defence Council, and it talks about the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. There is a distinction which is perhaps why the gentleman wasn't brought into the picture, but perhaps some questions with respect to this might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up on counsel's question, as of this time in late April, early May, 1992, we've talked this afternoon there was the Mostar Municipal Assembly, that was a body that dated back to at least 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The answer is yes, it did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we've discussed this afternoon something called the Mostar Crisis Staff, which I -- correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe you've indicated was established sometime after the JNA forces arrived in the Mostar region on approximately the 19th of September, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the answer to the question, Your Honour. I don't believe the gentleman indicated that back in 1991 the Crisis Staff was established. So perhaps we can get a clear date from the witness himself when it was established, because it's my understanding that the Crisis Staff derives from the Municipal Assembly and that the Assembly ceases to function as an Assembly once you have the Crisis Staff in place. Because there is a crisis, hence you can't have a hundred people managing the business of a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Karnavas's testimony, Your Honour, but if the witness could assist us. I believe he indicated earlier this afternoon that he could not put a precise date on it so I simply left it as open-ended as I could because I think -- I believe the transcript will show that it was sometime after the JNA forces arrived. If he can be more precise, I'm happy for the witness to be more precise on when the Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, with respect to the objection made by the Defence whether the Crisis Staff was substituted at the Municipal Assembly or by the Municipal Assembly, did the Crisis Staff replace the Municipal Assembly, in fact? You're nodding your head, but let's hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did. It took over the role, the leading role. I've said that several times, but I'll repeat it again since you insist: The Crisis Staff did take over the role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in order to assure Mr. Karnavas, when was that exactly? What date? What did the Crisis Staff replace the Municipal Assembly in the traditional line of work it did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope I'll satisfy Mr. Karnavas with my answer: Let me say the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've clarified that point now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that clarification, sir -- let me ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 00209.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as soon as you have that, sir, can you tell the Judges what that document is, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Could you zoom in, please, so I can see it, see the whole document. Or zoom out. Yes, I have seen this document. And this document -- or, rather, it's an order from Mr. Jadran Topic where he is relieving of duty the Crisis Staff of Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any information at the time, sir, that is in -- around the 15th of May, 1992, on what authority and on what legal basis Mr. Topic, Jadran Topic, purported to dissolve the Mostar Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't think there was any legal foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to paragraph numbered 3 under the order. It says: "Until the government referred to in paragraph 2 of this order is formed, the Special Purpose Council of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens." Now, with that in mind, could I please ask the registry to go back and display Exhibit number P 00190. My question to you now, sir, is we looked at this document earlier, but when you received the order dated the 15th of May relieving you and disbanding the Mostar Crisis Staff, did you understand that this Special Purpose Council essentially took over your function?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I didn't know about this document. It was a confidential document, the decision to establish the Special Purpose Council, that is. And I didn't know that it would be taking over the task of the Crisis Staff. I would have preferred it if they told me that loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges in your own words, why do you understand or believe that you were removed as the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
