utterances.text: Well, probably there were people who were far more capable of doing the job, of taking over the function of managing the town than I was, in the position I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that, sir? Did anyone come and meet with you and tell you that you were being relieved on that basis?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, they didn't. It might have been better if they had the wisdom to come and tell me and say, "Thank you for your work so far, but as of today we're going to appoint somebody else to replace you." But they didn't do that. They didn't make that human gesture, which I might have accepted as an elegant gesture and a solution that we would all agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but on the 15th of May we have this decision which you have in front of you, which you're looking at, and I assume that you had an office in the mayor's building, you had a secretary, you had a telephone. On the 16th of May you were in your office. On the 17th and 18th of May -- or did they prevent you from going to your office and replace you? You can tell us exactly what happened after the 15th of May. Did you stay at home? What did you do? Did you go to your office? What?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Not only that, we were all there together in a very nice office, very nice premises which used to be the rectorate of the university in Mostar, and we used it during that period as a place from which the Crisis Staff functioned so that, up until this decision was taken, we worked quite normally in that premises. Without any warning whatsoever, I came to the door that morning, the door was locked, and I was told that we no longer had access to the building. And that's how the role of the Crisis Staff ended; very abruptly. And after that I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but at the time there was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't inform Sarajevo, the authorities, of what had happened in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, as to communication with Sarajevo, communicating with Sarajevo, I had to go to the radio hams if I wanted to communicate with Sarajevo and tell them that I was alive and well. Everything else was down. All the other communication systems were down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in Mostar on the 15th of May, 1992, were there any representatives of international organisations such as the international press, foreign journalists? Did you have the possibility of alerting the international community in any way of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, at that time point in time, no. No communication whatsoever. No visits. Before there were the heavy clashes and the whole town was aflame, I don't know whether you can imagine what the atmosphere was like. But never mind. Let me try and go back to that period of time. I'm not going to go back to that period time because I find it difficult to talk about it. Anyway, all attempts in any way did not bear fruit. They weren't considered to be reasonable, because everybody in their own heads had their own concept for a solution, and everyone tried to impose his own solution as being the best. Some people put the carrot before the donkey, others resorted to the stick. But whatever the situation, it was a chaotic situation, a nightmare, and you didn't have any way of doing anything to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the President's question, did you have on any occasion, either shortly or any time after your removal, to communicate this information to Mr. Kljujic or to any other senior party officials in the HDZ-BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Everything was quite clear after the decision. Everybody knew what had happened in Mostar and how the situation was transformed overnight. And I have to add that the Bosniak side had nothing against doing things differently than they had been functioning -- than the way they had been functioning. And later on -- or one year later they had some provisional government which functioned in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness be shown Exhibit P 00219.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as soon as you have that, sir, let me ask you did you see that document around this time, involving the establishment of various departments of the HVO municipal government?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that when they shut the door in my face, shut the door to my office, I made no further attempts to deal with the problem that was a continuous one. And I might have even felt relieved of the heavy burden that I otherwise felt my job to involve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can I ask your -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the registry to show you now Exhibit P 00221.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would ask you, sir, first of all, again, did you around this time have the opportunity to see the appointment of various individuals to the positions in the HVO municipal government?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll nonetheless direct your attention to it for a moment, sir. Is it correct that, looking at this document, the person listed as number 3, Mumin Isic, was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. He's a Bosniak today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And person number -- the person listed as number 5, Senad Kazazic, is that person a Muslim, or a Bosniak by today's terminology?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sejo Maslo, number 6, also a Muslim of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 8, Hamdija Jahic, also a Muslim or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Jaganjac, person listed as 12, a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, he's not from Mostar, but I have met him so I can say that he's a Bosniak, too, yes, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, of these five Muslims that are listed on this document P 00221, had any of those Muslims been Muslims that were on the Mostar Crisis Staff at the time that it was disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection, then, with the implementation of these various decisions --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have to correct myself. I do apologise. I made a mistake. I don't know whether Viktor Stojkic was. I'm not quite sure. So it's possible that Viktor Stojkic was involved in the Crisis Staff. Not directly as a member of the Crisis Staff but in the name of the police, as a participant in the functioning of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is Mr. Stojkic a Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Ah, yes. You were referring to Muslims. I do apologise. Well, it's my mistake again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in reference to the 20 -- the decision dated the 29th of April, 1992, and the decision by Mr. Topic on the 15th of May, 1992, disbanding the Mostar Crisis Staff, can you tell us during these events what role, if any, the HVO military police played.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: We didn't have that notion and concept in our communications. The military police was something that we did not hear of at that point in time. All I can say is this: According to the principles in crisis situations, the regular police force and its structures would activate their reserve force, and they would join the existing police structures and then work together in unison as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Prior to the time that it was disbanded, did the Mostar Crisis Staff have anything called military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't have any military police, but did you have any authority over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the gentleman that I mentioned a moment ago was the head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there may have been an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The head of the military police or the head of the civilian police, Mr. Gagro? The transcript says the person you mentioned a moment ago was the head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. He was the head of the police of Mostar in peacetime, and as such he was -- he became a member of the Crisis Staff to deal with internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But with your permission, I'd like to go back to the 15th of May. You discovered that your office was closed, the key was taken away. Why didn't you go and see the civilian police to ask them to help you in the situation? Now you're smiling. Is that because that was impossible, because the head of the civilian police would have been on the opposite side, on the other side? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but because that representative of the police force was with me in that same office. So I had no need to call him up. He was already there, and he understood the whole situation, but quite obviously his authority wasn't strong enough to change anything. He couldn't change matters that were defined by that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, sir, the person that you've been referring to in the last few minutes as the head of the civilian police, that was Viktor Stojkic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, unless any of the Judges have any questions on this particular series of questions, I'm moving forward to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to know a bit more precisely what your reaction to this situation is. Obviously now there is a long temporal distance. You are telling us this with a voice as if it was an operetta, but I suppose it was not. Did you expect this to happen? Did you expect to find your office shut to you one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was highly probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honour. If we can go back and have the gentleman look at the preamble and maybe comment based on the question that you just posed. The preamble - I have a clean copy so he can read it if necessary - and perhaps that might help you with further questions on this particular matter because I think he was never given the opportunity to talk about the period which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. This was in later May, and the decision, the document we're talking about, has a preamble which refers to, I quote: "The statutory decision on the establishment of temporary executive power and administration in the territory of the HZ-BH, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the municipal HVO hereby proposes the following decision." I wonder whether actually "proposes" is a very adequate translation. So were you aware that an alternative, concurrent executive power had been established or declared or assumed or whatever you want to call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not. I was not made aware of the existence of any such document by way of any communication methods nor was any hint of any such document made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you were then practically operating in May in an informational vacuum. You didn't have an idea of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely no idea. As I said a while ago, we were living a bit a chaotic situation which perhaps is hard to imagine for people who did not experience that situation themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So I still find it a bit difficult to visualise this. You went, up to the 15th May, you went to your office and "governed the city," where in fact there was no power left to you. Did you not realise this, or did you not seriously attempt to govern the -- the affairs of the town? Can you -- can you explain a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you actually comprehended this in the right way. We were aware of the fact that the defence forces that were defending the city and seeking to organise life in the city were not cooperating with the Crisis Staff, and that was the result of the -- this decision of theirs which was presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you can see a person, a man proposing his own self as candidate for president, nominating his own self.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear to what you are referring now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you take a look at this decision, it is signed by Mr. Jadran Topic, who actually nominated himself, under number 1, as Jadran Topic, president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for a point of clarification, I was referring to actually the decision of May 15th where there is an extensive preamble. That's the -- that's the preamble that I believe if the gentleman was to be -- to look at, not this document, but I believe it's 209, where it has -- but the copy was illegible. That preamble sets out exactly the chaotic situation, I believe. Perhaps he could comment at this point, or we can clear it up on cross-examination, it doesn't matter. It would have been the other document, May 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have taken a lot of time now, and I suggest that you take it up in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just for the record, for clarification on the record, in reference to a question put by Judge Trechsel a moment ago, when you're talking about Mr. Topic appointing -- or excuse me, proposing or recommending himself as president, you're talking about Exhibit P 00221? Do you still have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this about Mr. Topic at this point: How was it that Mr. Topic was put in this position as president of the Mostar HVO? You were democratically elected in 1990. How was Mr. Topic put in this position, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Where he was an alternative to me. So whenever people could not -- when I couldn't see eye-to-eye to people and their stances, they would resolve their matters and take up matters with him. He was always there for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me -- hopefully, perhaps it will be the last question on this topic and we'll move forward, I know we've taken a lot of time, but if the witness could be shown again Exhibit P 00119. Did you learn around this time, sir, independent of the -- based on the document or independent of the document - I only point the courtroom to the document as a point of reference - did you learn around this time that Jadranko Topic had been appointed the president of the Mostar HVO by Mate Boban and Janko Bobetko? Did you learn that at the time that you were still the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, then, sir, was it -- can you tell the Judges, was it in approximately June of 1992 that the JNA and Serb forces left the Mostar -- at least, the city of Mostar and immediate surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I'd rather say that they fled the area, not left. But when they left, they withdrew to positions from which they could control the entire city. These are high elevations all around it which are -- which predominantly oversaw the zone of Nevesinje, which was -- which had a majority Serbian -- Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges when the Serbs and the JNA forces left the city of Mostar, was this done as a result of fighting, the taking up of arms by the HVO, including the Muslims against them, or did they depart the town, more or less depart -- as you said a moment ago, fled the town?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I believe that they could feel the danger, and they were aware of the fact that they could not remain on those positions, so that they actually withdrew from those positions a bit willy and a bit nilly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge or information at the time that the Serbs withdrew from the city of Mostar based on an agreement between the Croats and Serbs as opposed to being forced out of Mostar by military action?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you heard during this time period -- we're now again -- we've been talking about April, May, of 1992. In your position as mayor of Mostar, had you heard anything about the Graz Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Croats and the Serbs had been engaged in negotiations between themselves around this time? Did that come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When the JNA forces left Mostar, the city of Mostar, what happened to the Serb civilians in the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: They withdrew from Mostar for the most part. Some of the intelligentsia from among the Serbs in Mostar remained in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, can you give the Judges some estimate, please, in terms of the total Serb population in Mostar as of early June -- early, mid-June, 1992, what percentage of the Serb population left Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I should, if you'll allow me, like to use this opportunity to describe why Mostar was a multi-ethnic milieu. According to the 1990 census, 34 were Muslims, 33 were Croats, and 18 per cent were Serbs in Mostar, and 15 per cent were the others. At the time of the conflict and the withdrawal of the JNA, I suppose not more than 2 to 3 per cent of Serbs remained in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what happened to the Serb Orthodox cathedral or church in Mostar after the JNA forces left the city.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Regrettably, I myself witnessed this uncivilised act. It was destroyed. First it was set on fire, and then, after an interval of a day or two, the rest of the remaining walls were razed to the ground. I believe that not to have been a civilised act, something that our official authorities in Mostar should be proud of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know under whose command the forces were which destroyed the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question. It suggests that a particular force destroyed it. He can ask who destroyed it as opposed to leading and insinuating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The proper way to put the question would be to ask, "In your opinion or according to the information you have, who destroyed this Orthodox church?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, who do you understand destroyed the Orthodox church after the JNA forces left Mostar in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that, not an exact one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by "exact"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I object. Now we're asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He either knows or he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He may have a perfectly good answer, Your Honour, but unfortunately, unless I have a dialogue with the witness, I can't understand what he means by "exact" or "not exact."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put the question to the witness myself. There's an Orthodox church in your town, a church which was apparently destroyed. Who did that? People who lived in Mostar, people from the outside? In your opinion, who is responsible? Or perhaps you don't know. But if one is the mayor of a town, it's a little surprising if the mayor isn't aware of what's happening in his town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it is obviously hard to get to the bottom of the problem, because at the moment the JNA left the Mostar area, the immediate vicinity of the city, it had about 30 per cent more inhabitants than otherwise, than normally, because of the large influx of people into Mostar from all over the area, from the war-torn, war-ridden areas. So there was a huge crowd of refugees and other people coming to -- into the city. So it was very difficult to have an overall overview of the conduct of all those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that doesn't answer my question as to who destroyed the Orthodox church. You seem to be suggesting that refugees were responsible for that act. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is not what I'm suggesting. But the situation in which we found ourselves was hard to control. And one thing was certain, however: Whoever did that had to have explosives, because it was blown up by explosives and it was finished off by explosives. So that is the truth. Now, who did it and how and what particular explosives were used, this is something that I cannot say with certainty or confirm within my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Carry on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just inquire further. When you say you don't know or you don't know exactly, are you talking about you don't know the particular individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. Same objection. Now we're going to give him a smorgasbord of choices from which to pick. He doesn't know, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. This witness has never said he didn't know. He said he didn't know exactly. I don't know if that means he doesn't know the name of the individual who lit the fuse, or if he doesn't know the group, or if he doesn't know -- as you said, refugees. I'm just asking for more precise information from the witness, Your Honour. We don't know what he means by "exactly." If his question -- if his answer is, "I don't know the names of the individuals who did it," that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can assist us, please. You've heard the dialogue, you've heard the objections of Defence counsel, you've heard the Judge's questions. Can you provide us any more assistance? When you say you don't know exactly who destroyed the Serbian church, the Serb Orthodox church, can you tell us anything more? You said you saw it at one point. Can you tell us anything more about who was involved in destroying it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. I was an eyewitness but from a distance, as it were. I was not an onlooker. I wasn't watching as an onlooker. But the fact is that this was carried out at the time when there were no Serb force and this was an act that I did not approve of. It would, therefore, be good to say -- I should like to stress that -- that the city of Mostar never accepted, never countenanced what had been done to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you saying you as the mayor, the person who had just been relieved as mayor of Mostar, didn't countenance that, or how do you know about the position of Mr. Topic and others?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that question as well, Your Honour. Now we're suggesting that Mr. Topic was behind the blowing up of a church. I think it's highly suggestive and it's highly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. He just said -- the witness said -- the answer is the city of Mostar never accepted or countenanced that this had been done. Now we spent all afternoon with this witness telling us that by June, 1992, it was the Mostar HVO which had control of the city government. That's -- I haven't suggested anything other than what the witness has told us all afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "The city of Mostar" does not mean city government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned now, but I believe that my colleagues share my opinion, at this point in time we know that the Orthodox church was destroyed, but the witness says he doesn't know who did it. He says one should know who brought the explosives. It could have been the Serbs, the Muslims. It could have been the HVO, it could have been refugees or outsiders. We have no information about this. Everything else is just a matter of speculation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Changing topics, Mr. Gagro, did you ever hear of an organisation during this -- the time that you were mayor in 1991, 1992, named HOS, H-O-S?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that was -- were -- excuse me, yes, what the HOS was.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: In the multi-party system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, various parties were established and one of them was the HSP, which within its programme and composition had defined how to act under a defence position, defence conditions, and they established their defence forces and they were the H-O-S, the HOS. I think that's the abbreviation. They were military forces which acted through a particular party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may assist the Judges in the future, sir, if you can -- when you refer to this party organisation as the HSP, can you tell us what HSP stood for?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The HSP is the Croatian Party of Rights. One of the oldest parties that was ever formed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the relationship, if any, between -- strike that. What was the position or policy of HOS toward Muslims being members of HOS, or cooperation with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Since the HDZ controlled the HVO to all intents and purposes, which acted within defence structures in the Mostar area and further afield, the HSP also established and formed its own forces, and they were called HOS, and they, too, had ambitions and were ready to defend their thresholds. However, unfortunately those programmes were -- well, there was a discrepancy between the two, and they were acting each along their own courses, which were divergent. Now, your question as to whether HOS and the HVO acted along the same lines as a coalition or something like that. I think we can say quite openly and frankly that when General Kraljevic arrived in Ljubuski, he rallied the HOS forces and there was great sympathy for it, and many Croats who respected the HSP traditions intensively lobbied in support of HOS, of the HOS in our area. However, at one point in time they rather overstepped the boundaries of acceptability by those who were objectively stronger in the area, and what happened was there was a serious parting of ways as to how this knot should be resolved, Gordian knot between the HVO and HOS, their misunderstanding. Unfortunately, this general, General Kraljevic, who was the commander of HOS in Herzegovina, had a vision of his own. It was to cooperate with the Muslims and act jointly with the Muslims. And at one point in time he came to Mostar to talk to the leaders of the SDA, and on his way back to Ljubuski, he and his group of nine escorts were liquidated, and that's where the story ended, all this story about HOS and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. The courtroom clock seems to have stopped. I don't know if that's some sort of signal or not, but it seems to be five-twenty -- almost 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Looking at my watch, which is working, it's 5.25. So we're going to stop there, have a break, and resume at about ten to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, before the break you -- you had indicated on page 62, starting at line 6, you said: Concerning the HVO and HOS, "unfortunately, those programmes were -- well, there was a discrepancy between the two, and they were acting each other along their own courses, which were divergent." And then you went on with another narrative before we could ask you this question: In what ways or how were the courses of the HVO and HOS divergent or discrepant?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: The main difference was that the HVO believed itself to be the only military force active in the territory where the Croats lived, whereas the HOS wanted to take over that role. So initially they prevailed in Ljubuski, and they could have taken over the main defence role in Capljina, et cetera. So this was the main problem, as a result of which those two organisations, those two bodies didn't see eye-to-eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were they in competition with each other?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened to the HOS after Mr. Kraljevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, then they started lobbying their other leaders then, and some of them join the HVO willingly, others were forced to join them. They were then integrated within the defence force, and they acted in a joint manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving completely further ahead to 1993, I would like to direct your attention to the period of April and May of 1993. Where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Before the war, during the war, and after the war I lived in my flat in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated earlier that that was in what we call West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. In a central part of Mostar. I could even say in the elite part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately how far was your residence from the Bulevar and what became the confrontation line between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: At, well, between 4 and 500 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you observe happening along the Bulevar in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: What did I observe. Well, at the time after the JNA had withdrawn from Mostar and after temporary authority had been established in Mostar, life got back to normal, in a certain sense, and people could communicate with each other. There were no obstacles to such communication. If it was necessary for us to go to the left bank, we'd do so. Only the old bridge remained intact, so this is the bridge we used to cross over to the other side. So it was possible to communicate with the others. However, prior to the conflict that broke out between the Bosniaks and the Croats, immediately prior to that conflict you could see that there were opposing forces that were not fighting each other, but each night one side would stand on one side of the Bulevar and the other side would stand on the other side. And this was a sort of stalemate. And they would remain present at those sites until the morning, and in the morning they would simply withdraw as if nothing had happened. It was a little odd, but I can say for certain that that continued for perhaps a week. They were on opposite sides. I can't really tell you how they held their weapons, but they had taken up position at the Bulevar, and one of the parties was on one of the sides and the other on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn around this time that the HVO had made any demands concerning the location of an ABiH army unit in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I didn't learn anything about demands or ultimatums of any kind, but in part of the town that hadn't been affected by the lines I heard that there had been some explosions. In part of the town where there were no lines, there was some explosions. In the afternoon, about 5.00, this could be heard. Later, we found out that a group from the HVO had attacked the BH army's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this -- was this the headquarters that was located in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention specifically to the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, sir. And can you tell us what happened on those days, what you saw on those days.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, shooting broke out. That's all I could see. A conflict between the HVO and the ABiH broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any -- on the 9th of May, 1993, did you have any Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: They stayed on, but several days later - I can't say when exactly - some forces checked who was living in those flats, and those who were not of Croat ethnicity had to leave their flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever know or have any dealings with a man named Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And given the discussion that we had earlier today about the Kljujic group on the one hand and the Boban group on the other, in which of those two groups would you put Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, while there was -- while there were harmonious relationships in the HDZ, Kordic didn't have particular position, or perhaps his position was not enviable because he didn't have a job. And after some time had passed, Mr. Jerko Doko, as the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, told me that he had solved his problem and that he had appointed him to a position so that he could act within institutions that were responsible for defence in the area he lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you observe of the relationship between Mr. Boban and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Kordic was a very cooperative man, and when it was necessary to find solutions to certain problems, he was very active. He tried to impose some of his own ideas through those activities, but at the time it was already noticeable that he had opted to support Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, prior to the conflict that we've talked about today, did you know Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. A prominent citizen of Mostar and a much respected man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he as a youth the head of something called the Youth Organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: He was at the head of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the Youth Organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: These are nice memories for those who lived at the time. If communists had everything under their control, then it was necessary to allow someone to have some liberty so that that person could participate in active life. We had a lot of young organisation -- youth organisations, a lot of pioneer organisations, many such bodies. These were sort of ornaments that one could find attached to the Communist Party in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of education Mr. Prlic received in terms of a degree?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I know that he was a professor at the faculty of economy at the university in -- in Mostar. I'm not sure whether that's the case now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, from your knowledge, sir, during this time -- or even prior to this time, perhaps it was in the 1980s or the 1970s, what was the Socialist Union?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, so that one didn't have the impression that it was only the communists who were in charge of all policies in the former Yugoslavia, the communists found an elegant compromise which didn't pose a threat to them. One could say that the society was a democratic one, and this Socialist Union was counterpart to the communists, and all working people and citizens of Yugoslavia were part of this union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mr. Prlic part of the Socialist Union?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was too. And that was Prlic's first step towards his future political career that subsequently ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Prlic worked for, not only that he was a member but that he worked professionally for the Socialist Union?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but perhaps for a short period of time he was professionally engaged in the Socialist Union in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the Executive Council for Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: What was it? Well, a body that in fact implemented the decisions taken by the town Assembly. One says -- one calls it the Executive Board. It implements the conclusions and decisions taken by the town Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Mr. Prlic ever the president of the Executive Council for Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: When was that? Well, one year before the last multi-party elections that were held, because for one year Prlic was the deputy president -- the deputy Prime Minister of the BH government, and he left his position within the Executive Board and became deputy to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure he heard the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is one year after the elections that were held in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, could you assist the interpreters, please, by restating the name, if you did, of -- you said that Mr. Prlic was the deputy to Mr. Somebody. Can you repeat the name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Perhaps I was in a hurry. I wanted to clarify everything in one sentence. Mr. Prlic, after he had been appointed as president of the Executive Board of the Mostar Municipal Assembly remained in that position for about one year. Mr. Prlic can correct me if I'm mistaken, but that's my assessment, although, given all the time that has passed, it's difficult for me to be precise. After having held that position, he was elected as the Deputy Prime Minister of the Executive Board of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how long he remained in that position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I assume it was for about one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was Mr. Prlic working in Mostar when you -- during the time that you were mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. When I was elected, we met. I was invited to a discussion in Sarajevo. He still held the position of Deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had the responsibility to transfer power to the new authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina because Mr. Pad [as interpreted] had already left his position as Prime Minister of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Mostar, were you familiar with the fact that Mr. Prlic worked for a time apparently with a company apparently called Hepok?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry if I interrupt, but you were actually starting out asking for the name of the Prime Minister to whom Mr. Prlic was deputy. The name has just again not been understood by the interpreter, and perhaps we should get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, we're going to try again. Can you please very clearly state the name of this Prime Minister, if I understand correctly, that Mr. Prlic worked for or with for a time.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I assume his name was Gojko, his first name, but his surname was Ubiparip. This could be translated as someone who killed a horse. That would be one possible translation of his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly more information than we had before. All right, sir, let me go back to the question about Hepok, unless Judge Trechsel has another question. Let me ask you about this company called Hepok. Do you know for a time whether Mr. Prlic was employed with this company?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: At the end of his term of office in the former government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Prlic remained without a job. He returned to Mostar and found work in Apro. I think that's an abbreviation. I don't know what the full name is. This is a system that included many fields of activity in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you familiar with a company named Hepok; and, if so, what kind of a company was that? What business was it engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Hepok had vineyards and similar facilities, facilities for producing wine and many other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know what other lines of business this other company Apro was -- A-p-r-o, was that like a parent company to Hepok?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct. Apro had various fields of activities, and it acted as one company that unified all these various fields of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell the Judges, what position did Mr. Prlic hold during this time at this company Apro, or A-p-r-o?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but perhaps he was the director of that company, the chairman. I'm not sure if this is correct, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know if there ever came a time when Mr. Prlic was nominated or recommended for a position on the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, because I was an active participant in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you tell the Judges, please, what happened in that regard. And perhaps, first of all, you can tell us, was Mr. Prlic ultimately successful in being placed in that position as -- would it be the governor or a governor of the National Bank?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we didn't succeed. I'll tell you how he was put forward as a candidate and why he wasn't accepted as our candidate for the governor of the bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the initiative of the Prime Minister, the Croatian Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Croatian candidate was demanded for the position of the governor of the bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was for the Croats to put forward such a candidate. There were lengthy discussions about that, and as suggested by Mr. Jure Pelivan, who was the Prime Minister, Mr. Jadranko Prlic was proposed as a candidate. Knowing Mr. Prlic and his professional and organisational skills, knowing his qualifications, we were very happy to accept him as a candidate, but when designating this person, and this is a matter for the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were certain misunderstandings and he was withdrawn as a candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What led to him -- you said there were certain misunderstandings. Tell us what those misunderstandings were.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can tell you. An explanation would require more time. I don't want to tire the listeners, but I'll tell you. Every party, in its statute, has set procedure for selecting candidates for certain positions, the position that a candidate is being put forward for. Unfortunately, as is usually the case where we come from, everything was decided at the last minute, and when a formal -- when a candidate had to be put to the Assembly formally for adoption, it turned out that nobody had a very serious candidate to put forward. And finally, when Mr. Kljujic came to see us in Mostar, Mr. Pelivan came, too, and said that we had to put an end once and for all to this undefined candidacy, because it was a vital post for the functioning of the organs of power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had to have a candidate, they say. And then we said that the HDZ of Mostar was behind Jadranko Prlic. Mr. Kljujic wasn't delighted with the name of this candidate, and the explanation he gave was that the HDZ would not put forward anybody as candidate who was not a member of the HDZ. However, we insisted. We said, "Let's drop the formalities. Let's put this man forward and elect him, because he was a key figure and should be used to help solve the country's problems." And Kljujic was left in the minority, and he said, "All right. I won't insist upon you not putting Prlic forward as a candidate." He would remain from voting. So Mr. Prlic was put forward by us as a candidate. He went through the entire procedure to the commission for appointments that Mr. Prlic should be elected candidate. Mr. Prlic went through the commission proceedings and everything was on the table, ready for the meeting that was supposed to be held that day. And then -- well, I can say that Boban learnt about this, the name of this candidate, and he was opposed to it. And he started insisting that we should explain how it came about that we put Mr. Prlic forward was a candidate for that post. And finally it turned out that it didn't pass through the HDZ branch in Mostar and their meeting, that the procedure wasn't adhered to, and that therefore his candidacy could not be accepted. So then it was through their request that this proposal was withdrawn from the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a member of the HDZ, did you have any involvement in Mr. Boban subsequently appointing Mr. Prlic as the head of the finance department of the HVO or Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I had no information about that, nor, to be quite frank, was I delighted with Prlic's involvement along those lines. Well, let's leave that. That's my own personal opinion. I won't expound it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to have to ask you, sir, in light of what you've just said in the courtroom, is why were you not delighted with Mr. Prlic's involvement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Because all of us considered Prlic to be a man who was -- a man who had skills and was a good craftsman but didn't have sympathies for the HDZ. So this was a bit of a disillusionment that he had decided to involve himself in a programme which was led by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just consult my colleague, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no further questions for Mr. Gagro, and we thank the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 6.25. We have half an hour to go before 7.00. Mr. Kovacic, are you starting the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But before I do so, I'd like to allow my client, Mr. Praljak, to say something. He said he would take up not more than 15 minutes, and then I would like to resume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After that, I'm going to ask the registrar to tell us how much time the Prosecution had, how much time they used up. But anyway, Mr. Praljak, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagro, I'm Praljak. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak, to you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I would like to clarify certain points relating to the spring and beginning of summer, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Go ahead, ask me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1991, as you said, the Yugoslav People's Army arrived and the paramilitaries to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Let me just put you right. Perhaps I made a slip of the tongue. I used the concept of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Anyway, they come to Mostar, and there was a wave of 20.000 refugees coming before them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. They then took over the military structures, three-quarters of the area around Mostar. That is to say the hills and the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At that time in Mostar, the command of what we call forces, was he Mr. Berak [as interpreted]? Was the commander of what we refer to as forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he wasn't in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mean he was further afield?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, further afield.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Perak, was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just -- what forces? "We just call forces." Which forces with which organisation or which side or party, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's hear who the forces are. Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army and the Chetniks occupied Mostar and the surrounding hills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I can say that officially speaking it was the Titograd Uzice Corps that arrived in Mostar. That was what it was officially. Otherwise -- or that's what the Yugoslav army said. Now, who was in the composition of that force, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So as we were saying, those forces, the Uzice forces or whatever, we're going to refer to them as forces, the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, occupied Mostar, did they not, and that -- all the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite correct. They arrived in that first wave, that is to say on the 19th of September. They arrived, they reached Mostar, and they were armed to the teeth, but they entered in the region of the airport, the Heliodrom, and the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After that they occupied the hills on the right bank of the Neretva River towards Citluk and in-depth towards Siroki Brijeg; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. That was a process that evolved over a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as I have very little time, I'm going to try and get through my questions a little quicker. Thank you for your answers anyway so far. Now, did they on a daily basis bomb Mostar using heavy weaponry, heavy guns, heavy artillery in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when they started -- or let me put it this way quite simply: When the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started, they launched destructive attacks on Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perak -- Berak [as interpreted], the commander at that time, before my arrival, before I came to be the commander, did he issue an order at one point according to which the forces in Mostar should leave the Mostar area and withdraw towards the west and leave the entire area of Mostar to the forces of the Uzice Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. If it is seen that Mr. Perak issued an order of that kind, would it not be strange that you as the president of the Crisis Staff did not know about an order of that kind? Wouldn't that be a bit strange?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a bit strange, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that after that the Serb forces took Stolac and the Dubrava plateau, and on the 15th of May expelled from the eastern banks of the river Neretva to the right bank of the Neretva all or almost all of the population, both Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That is true, but I have to say that those same forces had previously conducted a massacre against the Croatian village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this expulsion on the 15th of May in Mostar, did it take place on exactly the same day when you --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It's a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I see, a coincidence. Thank you. How many people arrived on the left bank from the east bank? How many more people were expelled by this Uzice Chetnik force?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, nobody was allowed to stay there. And if they did, they fared badly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how many bridges in that short period of time were destroyed along the Neretva River from North Mostar to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: All of them except the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know who and in what way armed the people who voluntarily put their names forward to defend their houses in the Capljina-Mostar area? Who supplied them with weapons and how?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, mostly they purchased the weapons themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So were these volunteer units? Did anybody conduct a mobilisation before that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No. We referred to them as village guards, village watches.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how many such groups were there in the town of Mostar during the material period? That is to say April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Everybody capable of carrying a rifle rose up to defend their homes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know what functioned in Mostar at that point in time? Let's look at the bank, the waterworks system, electricity, arms, ammunition, supplies generally. Were they all functioning? Financial institutions? Banks, I've already said. Was that almost entirely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that it was all entirely destroyed. We did manage to save something, some of that, and the town -- or, rather, the municipality had 126.000 inhabitants, after all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when we look at Mostar itself at that point in time, and we're talking about the 15th of May, you couldn't take the road to Capljina and down to the coast. You couldn't go to Stolac by road. You couldn't go to Nevesinje by road. You couldn't go to Jablanica and Sarajevo by road. You couldn't go towards Citluk by road, and you couldn't go to Siroki Brijeg by road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was there only one road that was passable, that you could go to Mostar -- to and from Mostar on that one road?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that one road, was it covered by the artillery of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, it was, and I think that about 15 people lost their lives. Fifteen Mostar citizens were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And that was the only road that supplies could come into Mostar; what we ate, what we used to shoot with, and everything else that the town needed, that the 126.000 inhabitants of the town needed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. It was a very great problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me repeat: So every day during that period of time the Serbs were shooting at the town. There were wounded and there were dead.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Excuse me, but I'd like to define that by saying there was general chaos, general chaos reigned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, chaos. And as you say in the document we looked at here, we had anarchy, anarchy and terrorism. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, in a certain form, yes. But I think as far as terrorism is concerned, we can't take terrorism as being the right concept in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that during that period of time I myself was the commander of that part of the battlefield, from Capljina to the northern stretches of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I think we met, came across each other on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that already in the month of April, 1992, people were getting ready to leave the western part of Herzegovina - Citluk, Medjugorje, Capljina - because they were afraid of the danger that loomed and the poor state of the forces of the Croatian Defence Council, their lack of organisation? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, but I would doubt that. We weren't that prone to fear in order to run away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, do you know that each municipality dug trenches right in front of their municipal boundaries?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, when we spoke a moment ago, we asked the HVO and certain municipalities to establish communications so as to organise things in a simpler manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you think that it was simple, given that brief space of time, to link up and organise all those forces with all the problems that existed, that you know were in existence, for them to be able to in the month of June be ready, first of all to expel the Serb forces from the right bank of the Neretva River and then, some ten days later on, a long way from Mostar both towards Stolac and Northern Mostar? Would that have been easy?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Not at all easy, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When we say the Serbs left - we say that quite often - I'm sure you can appreciate my sentiments here, how many lives did that cost our soldiers, the fact that the Serbs left and to reach that goal?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I'm sure he know that better than me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we therefore consider, judging by the number of dead and wounded, the casualties we had on our side and that the opposite side had as well, that this form of conflict and clash by a military clash of two military formations --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I'm not following you. I didn't understand what you meant there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If we have dead and wounded on both sides, casualties on both sides and fatalities on both sides, can we call this a military conflict and not, just strolling, the Serbs left or went?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know who used that verb "left" or "went." I don't use that term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more brief questions. You said that Mr. Perinovic was replaced, and then rumour had it that that was because there was a Serb in his family, a Serb family member. But Mr. Kljujic was replaced as well, and he had no Serbs in his family. And then there was Brkic and some others. Now, can we therefore consider that Perinovic was not replaced for that particular reason?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, I can't go into that. Objectively speaking, it was very early on, and it was a rumour that went round when I was active.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now a private question. Was the sole remaining bridge across the Neretva River the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, when the Serbs were expelled, was it protected?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge in the heat of battle of the job of protecting the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Kovacic, with respect to the questions that were asked, I'd like to ask the witness: You said you met Mr. Praljak on one occasion. Do you remember when that was? When did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume -- it's difficult for me to pinpoint the exact time, whether I had already been replaced or not, I can't be sure about that, but I do know that Mr. Praljak invited me for talks. We had courteous talks. He said that he respected the legally elected organs in Mostar and that he had appointed a man whom we referred to as a liaison officer. Unfortunately, that liaison officer never appeared in our Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have another question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to clarify something. Mr. Praljak had put a question to you and asked you whether you knew who had protected the old bridge in Mostar. I didn't quite understand your answer. Did you know who was protecting the bridge or not? Was the bridge still intact when the Serbian troops withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The old bridge was in a fairly good state when the Serbian forces were driven out of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were there troops or was there a group that protected this bridge or was it just left intact without their engagement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, in the fight -- in the conflict between the JNA and the units defending the town, everyone moved over to the left side, and everyone participated in escorting those gentlemen into the hills. And afterwards, well, I don't know who stayed on to protect and defend that bridge which was the only bridge that linked the left and the right side of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Gagro, my name is Mr. Kovacic. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Praljak. There are a few other questions I'd like to put to you. Since we're discussing the old bridge, let me put another question to you about it. You said quite clearly that the bridge was in a fairly good state but it had been damaged. Could this damage be seen with a naked eye or was an expert required to see such damage?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, it was possible to see the damage to the armour, to the protection for the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the cause of that damage was?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious: Our forces had already taken up position around the old bridge, and that was the only link between the two sides, and Serbian forces shelled that position because they knew that forces would assemble there and that was the only point at which it was possible to cross from one side of the town to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So does this mean that the old bridge was damaged by the Serbian forces, by the Serbian artillery when the Croats and Muslims under the HVO organisation launched an offensive against the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, look, I have to correct you because I do know that, unfortunately, my colleague was killed on the bridge as a result of a mortar shell. It wasn't easy for the Serbs who had withdrawn to their positions to use guns and other artillery to target such a bridge, so they used mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was there any damage prior to that battle?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me about peacetime, well, you know that the old bridge in Mostar is one of the oldest bridges. It's existed for over 400 years. And it had been slightly damaged because of exposure to the weather, the rain. So it had been repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I wasn't very precise. You started talking about the history of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't know what you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My question concerned the time prior to when the bridge was damaged as a result of conflicts. But when the Serbs were in control of the town and when there was shooting, was the bridge damaged on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, that's possible, but it wasn't that visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. At the beginning of your testimony, page 9, line 19 of the transcript, you mentioned the establishment of the HDZ, and you mentioned the sister relationship between the BH HDZ and the HDZ in Croatia. You and I know what is at stake, but let's try to clarify this for others who are not that familiar with the situation. Do you remember when the HDZ was established in Croatia for the first time? I know you can't mention dates.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: In 1989. I know quite a few details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very good. The HDZ was established in 1989 in Zagreb, and at the time there were no conflicts and Yugoslavia was the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and was still in existence. It was still functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And other peoples and political groups at the time started founding the first free parties in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the SDA was established at that time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the period of time, those parties acted within Yugoslavia. The HDZ didn't have to restrict its activities to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Well, that was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that its political force was most felt in Croatia because that's where the Croats lived, however, it was active in other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that towards the end of 1989 and at the beginning of 1990 the HDZ established its branches in other European countries?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that such branches existed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were aware of the fact that the HDZ had been established. When was it established in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: It was certainly before the first multi-party elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time that Yugoslavia was still in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time - and we're still referring to the same territory regardless of the existence of republics - at that time was there formal, legal distinction to be made between the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HDZ in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I think that that's how they wanted to organise things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: All the HDZ in Croatia became active in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was believed that republics were zones in which Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina had their interests and Croats in Croatia had their own interests. So as to avoid any overlapping, the tendency was for the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be organised on principles that would enable this body to develop its political platform independently and in a way that it thought was most appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this explanation, is that why you say that these parties were sister parties? Is that based on that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you were a politically active man at that time, could one say that the SDA was also present not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in Croatia, too, since there were many Bosniaks, or at the time Muslims, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: I assume that it was in their interest to act in that way so as to assemble their own people, to have them support a programme that they supported, but I didn't really follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I know that you are not informed of the details. This took place 16 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes. And this was the very beginning of these events, and we didn't all intensively follow the establishment of new political parties. This was something new for the citizens of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But I think that your answer implies the following: Do you remember that the SDA also had branches of its own that were active in Croatia? I'm asking you this for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO
utterances.text: Yes, they did have such branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for instruction. Actually -- I'm sorry. I'm supposed to speak Croatian. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm in a bit of a dilemma. I could move on to another subject now, but I think it would be best if we proceed in a different manner. I'd like to show the witness some photographs, so perhaps it would be best to stop here and continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's almost 7.00 p.m. now. As far as the time you have tomorrow is concerned, according to the calculations made, the Prosecution has used up 2 hours and 44 minutes. The Judges took up the remaining time when putting questions to the witness. So in theory, the Defence should have the same amount of time. That means around three hours. Last week I asked you to discuss the matter among yourselves. I don't know what you have decided with regard to this witness. Could you tell me how much time you will need. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that we should be able to manage our time within the three-hour period, give or take a minute or two. Having said that, can we then assume that the witness that's to follow, that we are to be ready tomorrow afternoon, since we're going to -- I understand we're going to start at 4.00. Should we be ready to cross-examine the following witness that was supposed to return, because he should be back. My preference would be to go ahead and continue and use up the time, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, the witness who will be coming back, I thought he would be coming back on Wednesday. Tomorrow it's Tuesday. Mr. Scott, do you have any information you could provide us with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. As you know, we're prohibited from talking to the witness so we've had absolutely no communication with Mr. Smajkic, so I have no idea what his plans are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could make an inquiry. I'm sure that he would be travelling tomorrow. If he's here around noon or so, that would give him sufficient time and we can just go ahead. I don't see the reason to wait until Wednesday to commence with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. As you know, we'll stop at half past twelve tomorrow. We will then have a break until 4.00 p.m. because the Judges have a Plenary to attend, and we will then resume at 4.00 p.m. tomorrow and work until 7.00 p.m. Things will be a lot clearer tomorrow. The registrar has also reminded me of something that's unclear in the English transcript. He's drawn my attention to the fact that there's something that's unclear in the transcript. Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session? Fortunately, I still have my reflexes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 7.00 p.m. The clock has disappeared. I hope the registrar will provide us with a clock tomorrow, a Swiss one, I hope, thank you, and I'll see you all tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
